objectives.text: Explain balance, moderation and variety as working principles rather than slogans.
Say what the Dietary Guidelines are for and who they are written for.
Distinguish EAR, RDA, AI and UL, and say which one an individual should aim at.
Read a Nutrition Facts panel: serving size, %DV, and what 5% and 20% mean.
Judge a nutrition claim in the media against the evidence behind it.

terms.gloss: Recommended Dietary Allowance — meets the needs of about 97–98% of healthy people. This is the individual target.
Estimated Average Requirement — meets the needs of half a group. A research and planning figure, not a personal goal.
Adequate Intake — used when the evidence is too thin to set an RDA.
Tolerable Upper Intake Level — the most you can take routinely without expecting harm. A ceiling, not a goal.
A label figure based on a 2,000-calorie reference diet. Roughly: 5% or less is a little, 20% or more is a lot.
The amount the label's numbers describe. Every value on the panel is per serving, not per package.

questions.prompt: Which Dietary Reference Intake should an individual use as a personal target?
options: The RDA
The EAR
The UL
The AMDR
questions.why: The RDA is set to cover nearly all healthy people. The EAR covers only half a group, so aiming at it means a coin-flip chance of falling short.
distractorNotes: Meets the needs of 50% of a group — a planning figure, not a personal goal.
A ceiling to stay under, not a target to reach.
A range for energy-yielding nutrients, not a single intake target.

questions.prompt: What does the Tolerable Upper Intake Level describe?
options: The most you can take routinely without harm
The intake meeting the needs of most healthy adults
The point above which a nutrient stops absorbing
The largest amount the body can store at once
questions.why: The UL is a safety ceiling. Sitting between the RDA and the UL is fine; routinely exceeding the UL is where risk begins.
distractorNotes: That describes the RDA.
Absorption often continues past the UL; the concern is toxicity.
Storage capacity is a different idea entirely.

questions.prompt: A label says 20% DV for sodium. Per the label's own rule of thumb, that is:
options: A lot of sodium in one serving
A little sodium in one serving
A fifth of the sodium in the pack
A fifth of your own daily limit
questions.why: 5% DV or less is a little, 20% or more is a lot. The figure is per serving and against a 2,000-calorie reference, not against your personal limit.
distractorNotes: That is the 5%-or-less end of the rule.
Percent Daily Value is per serving, not a share of the package.
It is against a 2,000-calorie reference diet, which may not be yours.

questions.prompt: A package holds 2.5 servings. You eat the whole thing. The calories you consumed are:
options: Two and a half times the label value
Exactly what the label figure states
Half of the figure the label states
Impossible to work out from a label
questions.why: Every number on the panel is per serving. Eating the container means multiplying by the servings it holds — the most common label-reading error there is.
distractorNotes: The label figure covers one serving only.
Multiply, do not divide.
The servings-per-container line makes it a simple multiplication.

questions.prompt: Which best captures 'moderation' as the chapter uses it?
options: Eating any food in a sensible amount
Removing unhealthy foods from the diet
Eating the same balanced meals daily
Eating only at strictly regular times
questions.why: Moderation is about amount, not prohibition. Variety and balance are the companion ideas — no single food group carries everything.
distractorNotes: Elimination is a different principle, and rarely a sustainable one.
That is closer to the opposite of variety.
Timing is not what the term refers to.

questions.prompt: Who are the Dietary Guidelines for Americans primarily written for?
options: Healthy people from age two upward
People already diagnosed with disease
Athletes in structured training
Infants in their first year of life
questions.why: They are population-level guidance for generally healthy people. Clinical diets for existing disease are a separate matter.
distractorNotes: Therapeutic diets fall outside general population guidance.
Athletes have specific needs that sit on top of this.
The earliest years are handled separately.

questions.prompt: An advert cites 'a clinical study' with no author, size or comparison group. The sound response is:
options: Treat the claim as unsupported for now
Accept it, since a study was cited
Reject it — supplement claims are false
Try it and judge by how you feel
questions.why: A citation you cannot check is not evidence. Who ran it, how many took part, and what it was compared against are the questions that decide what it is worth.
distractorNotes: Naming a study is not the same as producing one.
Overcorrection — some claims do hold up.
Personal response cannot separate effect from expectation.

questions.prompt: Why is an AI set for some nutrients instead of an RDA?
options: The evidence is too thin for an RDA
It is needed only in very small amounts
It has no known toxic ceiling as yet
The body can synthesise enough itself
questions.why: An Adequate Intake is a best estimate used where the research does not yet support calculating an RDA. It is about evidence, not the nutrient's size or role.
distractorNotes: Trace nutrients can still have an RDA.
Having no UL is a separate matter.
Nutrients the body makes may not be essential at all.

questions.prompt: Why does variety matter even when calorie needs are already met?
options: No one food group has every nutrient
Because eating one food becomes dull
Because calories differ between foods
Because variety slows digestion down
questions.why: Different foods carry different nutrient profiles. Meeting energy needs says nothing about whether the six nutrient classes are all covered.
distractorNotes: True enough, but not the nutritional reason.
A calorie is a calorie; the nutrients alongside it differ.
Not the principle at work here.

questions.prompt: On a Nutrition Facts panel, which figure should you read first?
options: The serving size
The calorie count
The total fat line
The ingredient list
questions.why: Serving size sets the scale for everything below it. Reading calories before checking the serving is how a 200-calorie snack turns out to be 500.
distractorNotes: Meaningless until you know what serving it describes.
Same problem — it is a per-serving figure.
Useful, but it is not part of the panel's numbers.

checklist: Pick a packaged food you actually ate this week.
Write down the serving size and how many servings you really had.
Multiply the calories, sodium and added sugar by that number.
Name one line on the panel that surprised you, and say why.
selfCheck: Did I multiply by servings actually eaten, not servings on the label?
Did I use the 5% / 20% rule rather than eyeballing it?
applicationPrompts.aiPolicy: These are questions for you to answer. This app does not write any part of a submission.
